criteria.descriptor: Correctly names real LLM-as-judge biases (position/order, length/verbosity, self-enhancement) with valid mitigations, correctly distinguishes a pairwise preference win rate from capability benchmarks, applies sound statistical reasoning (CIs/sample size), and invents no fake mechanisms. Full marks require identifying length bias as specifically dangerous given DPO's tendency to lengthen outputs.

Covers the full validation surface - judge-bias controls, statistical significance, contamination/representativeness, capability AND safety regression (alignment tax), and substance-vs-style - rather than fixating on one dimension. Partial credit scales with how many of these axes are addressed.

Explains WHY each risk threatens the 68% conclusion (e.g., why DPO's length increase confounds the judge, why chat win rate can't detect a reasoning regression) and ties the mitigations into a defensible, explicit ship/no-ship gate rather than listing checks in isolation.

Communicates as a prioritized set of risks each paired with a concrete mitigation, uses correct post-training vocabulary (DPO, LLM-as-judge, length-controlled win rate, alignment tax, IFEval), and ends with a clear recommendation suitable for a design review.

expected_answer_points: Position/order bias in the LLM judge: evaluate each pair in both orderings (swap A/B) and average or require the win to hold under swapping, rather than trusting a single fixed order.

Length/verbosity bias is the key confound because DPO systematically lengthens outputs and judges favor longer answers; report length distributions and use a length-controlled win rate (e.g., AlpacaEval 2.0) so the gain isn't just verbosity.
A single judge is insufficient (self-enhancement/familiarity bias): corroborate with a second judge family and/or human spot-checks, and report judge-human agreement.
Statistical significance: 68% needs a sample size and a confidence interval (e.g., bootstrap over the held-out prompts) whose lower bound clears 50% before it counts as an improvement.

Alignment tax / capability regression: pairwise chat preference doesn't capture reasoning or knowledge, so run standard capability benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, IFEval) on both checkpoints and gate on no regression.
Contamination / representativeness: verify the held-out instructions don't overlap the DPO preference data and match the production distribution rather than easy chat prompts.

Substance-vs-style / reward-hacking and safety: inspect wins to confirm they're driven by correctness not formatting/tone, and run safety and over-refusal evals since preference tuning changes refusal behavior.
common_pitfalls: Accepts the 68% as self-evidently a real improvement and recommends shipping, treating the win rate as ground truth instead of a biased, noisy measurement.
Fixes only position/order bias while ignoring length/verbosity bias, which is the dominant confound because DPO reliably produces longer answers that judges prefer.

Stays entirely within chat win-rate framing and never checks capability regression (alignment tax) via benchmarks like MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval/IFEval, so a reasoning/knowledge regression could ship unnoticed.
Omits any statistical treatment - no confidence interval or sample-size reasoning - or conflates 'statistically significant' with 'practically meaningful.'
Proposes 'just use a stronger/bigger judge model' as if a better judge removes systematic biases like length and position, which it does not.
Assumes a 'held-out' set automatically means no contamination and representative coverage, without checking overlap with the DPO preference data or the production prompt distribution.
reference_answer:
A single 68% LLM-as-judge win rate is a signal, not a verdict; I'd validate it along several axes before signing off.

Judge biases. Pairwise LLM judges have systematic biases. Position/order bias: the response shown first is often favored, so I'd evaluate each pair in both orders and only count a win when it survives swapping (or average the two orderings). Verbosity/length bias is the dominant risk here because DPO reliably lengthens outputs and judges reward length; I'd report both models' length distributions and use a length-controlled metric (e.g., AlpacaEval 2.0's length-controlled win rate) so the gain isn't just 'longer.' Self-enhancement/familiarity bias means one judge is not enough, so I'd corroborate with a second judge family plus a human spot-check and report judge-human agreement.

Statistical validity. 68% is uninterpretable without sample size and a confidence interval. I'd compute a bootstrap CI over the held-out prompts and require its lower bound to clear 50% with margin; typically a few hundred prompts.

Representativeness/contamination. I'd confirm the held-out instructions don't overlap the DPO preference data and that they match production traffic, not just easy chat prompts.

Alignment tax/regression. Pairwise chat preference says nothing about knowledge or reasoning, and DPO/RLHF can silently degrade base capabilities. I'd run capability benchmarks on both checkpoints - MMLU, GSM8K/math, HumanEval, IFEval (instruction following) - and gate on no regression. I'd also run safety and over-refusal evals, since preference tuning shifts refusal behavior.

Substance vs style. I'd read a sample of wins to confirm they're driven by correctness and helpfulness rather than formatting, hedging, or tone (reward hacking / Goodhart).

Sign-off gate: a length-controlled, order-swapped win rate with a bootstrap CI whose lower bound clears 50%, no capability or safety regression across the benchmark suite, and human confirmation that wins reflect substance - not just a raw 68%.
